full_judgment:
14. Mr. A. H. Mahfuzur Rahman, the learned Advocate has appeared for the appellant. He has submitted that no cause of action had arisen for filing the suit against defendant No.4. In absence of any cause of action against defendant No.4, the plaintiffs suit cannot be decreed. He has further pointed that the plaint was amended on 28.1.1999 by Order No.31 impleading Md. Serajul Islam as defendant No.4, while suit was pending. Thus, no cause of action had been arisen to implead the defendant No.4 in the suit as has been inscribed in the averments of the plaint. He further added that the main suit was for Specific Performance of Contract in between the plaintiff and defendant No. 1. Therefore, it should be resolved whether there was a contract for sale and consideration money was passed or not. In such a nature of the suit there was no scope for further relief or reliefs praying for declaration that the deed in question registered in favour of defendant No.4 is cancelled and not binding upon the plaintiff is totally unfounded. It is in contrary to Section 42 of the Specific Relief Act. Therefore, the suit for specific performance of contract cannot be turned as suit under Section 42 of the Specific Relief Act and as such, the suit itself is not maintainable, He has further added that since the plaintiff himself impleaded Md. Serajul Islam as defendant No.4, he has locus sandi to tile the appeal as the judgment and decree has attracted his deed in question. He by referring Section 52 of the Transfer of Property Act and some precedents which are to the case of Bangladesh Leaf Tobacco Company Ltd., reported in 43 DLR 7 and to the case of H. M. Saya & Co.- vs - Nazer Ali Industries, reported in 21 DLR (SC) 50, has argued that admittedly the suit is not maintainable. He has further added that the suit is not maintainable in its present form as prayed for declaration that the sale deed No.747 dated 16.03.1997 in the name of defendant No. 4 is illegal, concocted and not binding upon the plaintiff in a suit for Specific Performance of Contract. So, the suit is defective as mis-joinder, the prayer of the suit cannot be treated as the suit for Specific Performance of Contract, rather, it turned to a suit for declaration which cannot and as such, the suit is not maintainable. According to him the provisions of Sections 101 and 103 of the Evidence Act contemplated specially to prove the facts who assert the same. So, from the averments of the suit and the evidence led by the plaintiffs side against defendant No.4 there is no cause of action and as such, the suit cannot be decreed against defendant No.4. He further pointed that none of the P.Ws. put their signatures in the alleged Bainapatra in presence of the plaintiff and defendant No. 1. Therefore the suit for Specific Performance of Contract cannot be decreed unless and until the signature of the executant is proved beyond all reasonable doubt and as such, the impugned judgment and decree is liable to be set aside. He has lastly submitted that in passing the impugned judgment and decree the Court below erred in law and as such, the same is liable to be set aside. 

 18. In the instant appeal the most important aspect of the suit as has been derived from the materials on record is that whether the written statement of the defendant No.1 would be considered ipso facto as evidence against the plaintiff without any oral testimony by defendant No. 1 himself or by any authorised person. Because, he was not examined as defendant No. 1 supporting his defence case as stated in the written statement rather, he was examined as D.W.4 as supporting witness on behalf of defendant No.4. 

 19. As we find from the record that at the time of deposition Abdul Gafur was cited as D.W.4 did not mention anywhere in his deposition that he has deposed for himself in support of his written-statement, rather, iris apparent from his examination-in-chief that he has deposed as D.W.4 as supporting witness on behalf of defendant No.4. So, from this way of viewing it is crystal clear that defendant No. 1 did not contest the suit although filed the written-statement. Therefore, according to as the filing of the written-statement without giving any oral testimony in support the same before the Court below and without facing cross-examination the same will not be considered ipso facto as evidence rather, according to us either of the pleadings must be proved by giving oral evidence. 

 21. From the above discussion, it is apparent that the defendant No.1 did not contest in the suit specifically denying the case of the plaintiff. Since, the defendant No. 1 did not deny the specific assertion made in the plaint, neither in the written-statement nor in evidence in Court, So, the case of the plaintiff deem to have been admitted by the defendant No.1 in accordance with the provisions of rule- III of order VIII of the Code of Civil Procedure. 

 So, it is crystal clear that Abdul Gafur admitted his signature in the Bainapatra, although the learned Advocate for the appellant pointed that none of the P.Ws. proved the signature of said Abdul Gafur in the Bainapatra in question. We are of the view that while executant himself in cross-examination admitted that he has signed in the agreement in presence of other witnesses who also examined in the suit as PWS .2 and 3, so, proving of signature of the executant by other witnesses is not necessary as required by law. Thus, it is our considered view that the signature in question in the Bainapatra is genuine. So, the contention advanced by the learned Advocate for the defendant appellant raising question regarding the genuineness of Bainapatra is nothing, rather contrary to the evidence on record.
